synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: 1 defining/development reference (1 programme) for the 2004 seven-dimension form; no subsequent complete-form primary programme retained in this bounded search. Separately retained: 1 earlier two-output gambling adaptation and 1 author-independent subsequent online two-output programme; 2 representative empirical applications of adapted forms. 2 relevant sources remain access-blocked.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
Evidence coverage is anchored to gambling-specific G-TLFB0009. The generic TLFB0120 family member was not fully searched. Alcohol/substance TLFB methods provide historical context, without transferring their reliability to gambling.

G-TLFB reconstructs gambling over a specified period using a calendar and meaningful dates. Its gambling-specific development study supports repeatability of several behavioural outputs and comparison with daily self-monitoring. These are separate outputs, including frequency, time and financial measures, rather than a single severity score.

The original evidence came from college gamblers. Strong correlations did not remove reporting differences: recalled frequency, own-money risk and alcohol use were lower than daily reports, and net financial outcomes showed weaker agreement. Both methods depended on self-report. Earlier gambling calendars and a later online gambler–collateral comparison provide useful supporting context, but used fewer outputs and different procedures.

The current search did not establish objective financial accuracy, a meaningful-change threshold or complete-form replication across clinical populations and administration modes. A recent treatment-outcome meta-analysis and a primary recall-bias study could not be read in full and are excluded from extracted evidence. Repeated use in treatment research therefore should not be read as validation of every shortened implementation or change score.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: State the recall window and calendar/event-aid procedure; shorter subsets of a longer calendar are not separately validated forms.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: Distinguish intended stake, own money risked and net win/loss; these are not interchangeable expenditure measures.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Retrospective reports can differ from diaries; proxy agreement does not establish objective accuracy.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Completion burden varies with gambling frequency and detail; online or shortened procedures require their own evidence.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Behavioural change can be described, but meaningful-change thresholds and objective financial verification were not identified in the retained anchor evidence.

synthesis.public_family_name: Canadian Problem Gambling Index / Problem Gambling Severity Index (CPGI/PGSI)
synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: PGSI anchor: 1 defining/development source · 5 subsequent primary study programmes (6 full-text publications; 4 author-independent programmes) · 5 representative examples of use.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
The nine-item PGSI has substantial population-survey evidence for a coherent total severity score and consistent items. Selected Canadian and British studies include teams without Ferris/Wynne author overlap. Some publications reuse datasets; the retained counts describe this bounded search, not the entire literature. Ipsos corporate authorship does not establish individual independence.

Evidence is less clear for distinguishing the original low- and moderate-risk categories. Item interpretation, participation filters and sampling methods affect comparisons. Agreement with an older DSM-IV screen is not proof of DSM-5 diagnostic accuracy or a complete inventory of gambling harms.

Development-stage retest and later long-term stability/change analyses are available, but they do not establish an anchor-based meaningful-change threshold for the unchanged twelve-month form. Language adaptations, short forms and sports-specific versions require their own evidence; clinical application alone does not validate treatment responsiveness.

This family page uses PGSI as the evidence anchor. CPGI package context and incidental three-item findings are separated. The sports-adapted form was not searched; no family-wide completeness is claimed.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: State the nine-item form, twelve-month window and scoring categories.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: Short follow-ups may cover overlapping recall periods.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Keep severity categories distinct from diagnosis and a complete harm inventory.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Report participation filters, sampling and scoring changes when comparing studies.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Check exact-language, short-form and outcome-change evidence for the intended use.

synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: Original-task anchor only: Evidence currently identified: 1 defining/development reference (1 programme); 2 selected subsequent primary methodological programmes (2 publications; both author-independent) using original-payoff tasks, including an awareness-probe modification; 3 secondary syntheses; 1 representative anchor application. Two later clinical-version programmes are contextual evidence. This bounded selection is not a literature total. One PDW adaptation reference/application retained incidentally.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
The IGT records choices from four decks while participants learn from gains and losses. Original development in people with focal brain lesions defined deck profiles and the advantageous-minus-disadvantageous net score. It provides evidence about decision behaviour under this task, rather than a direct gambling-harm measure or a test that uniquely isolates one mental process. Reward frequency, learning and knowledge of the decks can affect interpretation.

This bounded search retained two author-independent methodological programmes using original payoffs: a computer repeat-assessment study and an investigation with awareness probes. Raw performance showed limited repeat stability in the small student study; more stable computational parameters were different, model-dependent outputs. Two later clinical-version programmes are retained separately. Their weak score stability and practice effects should not be presented as coefficients for the original physical task.

Selected reviews show average IGT differences between gambling groups and controls, with variation in samples and task definitions. Such group associations do not establish individual diagnostic accuracy, causation of gambling harms or a unique latent construct. Healthy-adult synthesis also indicates population-related score differences. Evidence for universal comparability across software, payoff schedules, languages or populations was not established in this search.

Repeated exposure can improve performance without treatment. Individual reliable or meaningful change thresholds for gambling services were not identified in the current search. One retained gambling application illustrates use of the anchor task; post-decision wagering has separate, incidental adaptation evidence and its own scoring uncertainties. Only the anchor was fully searched.

The post-decision-wagering member was not separately searched to completion. Its adaptation paper concerns source-specific advantageous-choice and wagering outputs, not automatic transfer of canonical net-score evidence. CAL-I-01 closure approved a v1.1 correction to developer attribution and scoring specification while preserving the original v1 audit record.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: Record payoff schedule, deck labels, software/version, instructions, incentives and trial count; later clinical and wagering versions need their own evidence.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: State whether the outcome is a net score, deck/block count or computational parameter; these outputs have different meanings.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Learning and repeat exposure can change performance; account for practice before interpreting treatment-related change.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Group differences do not establish individual diagnosis, gambling-harm attribution or one uniquely measured construct; consider reference-population comparability.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Administration and access resources depend on the implementation; this search does not establish equivalent software, norms or current licence terms.
synthesis.family_synthesis_note: Anchor-only completed search. Clinical versions contextual; PDW incidental. CAL-I-01 closure approved the PDW v1.1 identity/specification correction. Blocked candidate excluded from public evidence counts.

synthesis.public_family_name: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)
synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: DSM-5 (2013) gambling-section anchor only. Current bounded selection: 4 defining/development or specification references (one overlapping framework-development context); 5 subsequent primary gambling-criteria study programmes (5 publications); 2 narrative syntheses; 2 representative applications. Two primary programmes involve named developers; author independence of the other three is unclear, so no confirmed independent subset is reported. Original manual is access-blocked and excluded from extracted counts. This is not a literature total.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
DSM-5 is a diagnostic classification reference used to guide clinical assessment. For gambling disorder, the 2013 edition specifies nine criteria and a threshold of four within 12 months, alongside clinically significant impairment or distress and a manic-episode exclusion. It renamed and reclassified the disorder, removed the separate illegal-acts criterion, and added criterion-count severity and course/remission descriptions. Official development documents and an authoritative criteria reproduction support this specification; the original manual was not accessible in this search.

Five selected primary programmes examined gambling-criterion classification, reliability, structure or severity. Much of this evidence used older questionnaire or interview responses recoded to the DSM-5 rule. It supports the threshold changes in those implementations, with moderate short-term count stability and evidence of a common severity dimension. High agreement between editions comes from shared symptom data; classification against treatment status uses an imperfect reference. These results are not coefficients for the manual as an administered scale. Two programmes include named developers; independence from the full APA contributor team could not be confirmed for the other three. Reused cohorts also mean programme counts are not independent-dataset counts.

Criteria have different statistical severity and importance, and some function differently across gambling populations. Studies of severity bands found that moderate and severe cases did not consistently differ in functional impact; a recent Spanish clinical network study also found sex-related criterion patterns. Interviews and self-report questionnaires implementing the same criteria can classify different proportions. The inspected general DSM-5 field-trial report did not provide a gambling-specific agreement estimate, and evidence for universally equivalent assessment across settings or languages was not established here.

DSM-5 diagnosis provides a classification of disorder, rather than comprehensive coverage of gambling harms: harm can occur below its diagnostic threshold. A cross-sectional severity difference does not establish reliable or meaningful treatment change, and these criteria are not automatically a short-window outcome scale. This completed calibration anchor focuses on the gambling-disorder section, with component evidence recorded explicitly. It does not imply validation of every DSM-5 diagnosis or transfer evidence to DSM-IV, DSM-5-TR or other DSM versions.

The family’s locked default remains DSM-IV (0108). The current evidence anchor is DSM-5 (0109); its gambling-criteria component (0184) has nested coverage. Other DSM editions and version-unspecified records remain unsearched, and their evidence cannot be inferred from this page.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: State the DSM edition and actual interview, questionnaire or clinical procedure; recoded DSM-IV responses do not directly test every final DSM-5 wording change.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: The diagnostic decision includes the 12-month window, impairment or distress and manic-episode exclusion; a bare symptom count or screen may omit these.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Classification concordance, clinician agreement and accuracy against an independent diagnosis answer different questions; check the reference used.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Criterion-count severity bands do not capture all gambling harms or automatically provide reliable or meaningful treatment-change thresholds.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Use requires clinical judgement and implementation-specific training/resources; consult authorised edition/access terms before reproducing criteria.

synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: PHQ-9 anchor only: Evidence currently identified: 1 defining/development reference (1 programme); 2 retained subsequent primary programmes (2 publications; both author-independent) for the specified nine-item form; 4 secondary syntheses; 2 representative application examples. Two German contextual programmes are retained separately. This bounded selection is not a literature total.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
PHQ-9 measures depressive symptoms over the previous two weeks. Original clinical development and a large external evidence base support consistent items, expected relationships with functioning and useful depression-screening accuracy. A positive score needs clinical assessment; the questionnaire does not establish whether depression was caused by gambling. Structural reviews generally support a total score, with qualifications for analytical method and comparability across languages and time.

This calibration uses four selected syntheses and a small set of primary programmes, rather than counting the full literature. The two counted subsequent programmes have no defining-author overlap: UK primary-care change research and a Spanish telephone/retest study whose administration language was not explicitly reported. German responsiveness evidence is retained as translated-form context. Samples, reference interviews and administration modes affect interpretation; the counts do not establish independent datasets or English-language replication in every study.

PHQ-9 can track depression over time, but patient-perceived improvement and change beyond measurement error answer different questions. A recent pooled error analysis used internal consistency rather than observed retest change and found substantial variation across settings. Neither its pooled threshold nor a primary-care perceived-change estimate is a universal rule for gambling services. Endpoint and change scores need defined visits, sign, analysis and missing-data handling.

Two gambling-related examples illustrate use. A German slot-machine-gambler trial also reports limited sample-specific internal consistency; that result is retained separately from application evidence. Dedicated gambling-population diagnostic, structural and repeatability validation was not identified in the current bounded search. The Swedish example evaluates a gambling interview using PHQ-9 as a comparator, rather than validating PHQ-9 itself.

Only the nine-item anchor was searched to completion. Endpoint/change members have incidental source-specific coverage. PHQ-4 and the Swedish PHQ-8 systemic-sclerosis member remain unsearched; no anchor findings or counts are assigned to them.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: State the nine-item form, language, mode and two-week recall window; shorter family members need their own evidence.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: Screening thresholds and severity bands are different from a clinical diagnosis and from attributing depression to gambling.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Define endpoint visit and change-score sign, timepoints, estimand and missing-data method; questionnaire evidence does not settle every derived outcome.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Separate patient-important improvement from change beyond measurement error; threshold estimates depend on population and method.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Gambling-specific evidence identified here is limited; do not assume diagnostic accuracy or cross-language/time comparability in gambling services.
synthesis.family_synthesis_note: FAMILY_ANCHOR bounded completion; aggregate counts explicitly describe selected anchor evidence, not every member. German context separate; no questionnaire evidence flattened onto derived outcomes.

synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: Current bounded anchor search: 2 defining/specification references in 1 development context; 2 subsequent primary programmes (2 publications; 0 author-independent): 1 psychiatric-module clinical reappraisal and 1 gambling-module consistency programme. One independent modified-form programme retained separately; 2 representative gambling applications. No gambling clinical-accuracy programme identified in this search.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
This family contains distinct CIDI versions and short forms. The current calibration fully searched WMH-CIDI0293 only, with a named DSM-IV CIDI3.0/NCS-R gambling-module evidence anchor. The psychiatric-module comparison and German modified gambling evidence are explicitly separated.

WMH-CIDI is a fully structured psychiatric interview administered by trained interviewers. For gambling, the evidence here concerns the DSM-IV CIDI3.0 module used in the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication and its posted schedule. It gathers lifetime symptom history and recency alongside gambling behaviour and treatment information. It is not a single summed severity scale.

The gambling symptom reports showed good internal consistency in the US survey, but the authors explicitly reported no clinical reappraisal of gambling diagnoses. A landmark clinical comparison supports agreement for named anxiety, mood and substance modules; those results do not establish gambling diagnostic accuracy. Both anchor measurement programmes involved developers, and their US components share the parent survey.

German PAGE research illustrates translated, modified telephone administration and shows why screening gates matter: restrictive loss gates could miss criterion-positive participants. That evidence concerns the modified implementation. Exact release, wording, diagnostic algorithm, reference period and population therefore matter. Gambling-specific repeatability and diagnostic-accuracy evidence were not identified in the current bounded search.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: Specify the WMH-CIDI release, gambling module, language, administration mode and diagnostic edition; CIDI short forms and other versions have separate evidence.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: Lifetime criteria, recent symptoms and gambling-behaviour outputs are different operationalisations; retain the exact algorithm and mania exclusion.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Screening gates, optional-module sampling and weights affect who is assessed and how population estimates are interpreted.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Clinical agreement for other psychiatric modules does not validate the gambling module; alpha does not establish diagnostic accuracy or retest stability.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Historical training/certification and permission requirements apply to the posted materials; check current access and support for the intended release.
synthesis.family_synthesis_note: STOPPING_RULE_MET: authoritative definition/module, mode/edition/recall/algorithms, landmark psychiatric agreement, explicit gambling consistency/gap, modified-gate sensitivity and two representative applications cover the public synthesis. Further broad CIDI validation or application accumulation is unlikely to change it; no exhaustive census. Gambling retest/inter-rater/clinical accuracy remain not identified in this bounded search.

synthesis.public_family_name: Gambling treatment engagement and retention indicators
synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: Anchor only: Current bounded search:2 defining/reporting references (including1 review);1 subsequent primary methodological programme (1 publication);2 overlapping secondary syntheses;2 representative applications;1 implementation resource. Author-independence comparison is not applicable to this generic service indicator; reviewed studies are not additional extracted programmes.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
Treatment dropout rate describes a source-defined proportion of people or treatment episodes ending before an expected endpoint. Services may define this through missed sessions, a minimum attendance rule, completion of a planned course or clinical judgement. Entry at referral, intake or the first treatment session also creates different denominators.

Two retained reviews show substantial variation in definitions and reported rates. Their overlapping evidence should not be added together as independent primary studies. A selected primary analysis found that some clients leaving an initial six-session block had already improved in depression; this does not establish sustained gambling recovery, but it shows why attendance alone can misclassify clinical progress.

Routine reporting can separate unscheduled exits from completed care, referrals, other discharges and episodes still open. A proportion among closed episodes differs from the chance of dropping out among all treatment starters. Direct exit-coding reliability and universal rules for pauses, transfers, re-entry, deaths or follow-up were not identified in this bounded search.

The indicator describes service engagement or process under its stated rules. It cannot establish why a person left, whether they recovered or the quality of care without additional information. Lower rates are not automatically better care, and comparisons require similar cohorts, endpoints, follow-up and coding.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: State numerator, denominator, treatment-entry rule and expected endpoint; distinguish referral/intake attrition, during-treatment dropout and follow-up non-response.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: Specify observation period, episode construction and handling of ongoing care/censoring; closed-episode percentages differ from starter-cohort risks.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Record voluntary versus service-initiated exits and separate transfer, agreed early completion, pauses/re-entry, deaths and administrative discharge where the data permit.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Document missing/unknown exit codes, duplicate episodes and service coverage; do not assume coding reliability from review-screening agreement.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Interpret completion alongside goals, symptom change and patient/service context; the rate alone supplies neither reasons for leaving nor a care-quality ranking.
synthesis.family_synthesis_note: Fully searched0519 only;0552 attendance not fully searched. Attendance is contextual to dropout definitions, not evidence that attendance and completion are equivalent. Sources and counts apply to stated dropout operationalisations; other family evidence coverage incomplete.

synthesis.evidence_currently_identified_line: Anchor only: Current bounded search:2 defining/specification references (1 empirical development programme);3 subsequent primary methodological programmes (3 publications);2 representative applications;2 implementation resources. Author-independence comparison is not applicable to this generic indicator; counts are not a literature census.
synthesis.family_evidence_narrative:
Net money lost is a monetary quantity calculated over a stated period. The retained sources use cash-based reconstruction, retrospective reports and operator-recorded bets minus winnings. An annual loss divided by12 is an average month, rather than a direct observation of the last month. Account deposits minus withdrawals measures a different cash flow.

Direct comparisons show that wording, recall, spending intensity, product mix and data cleaning affect self-reported estimates. Operator records provide a comparison within their covered accounts and products; they do not automatically cover gambling elsewhere. Proxy reports are also imperfect. Agreement findings belong to the particular source, window and reporting procedure studied.

Loss distributions can be highly skewed, and changing the treatment of extreme values or winnings can change summaries. Absolute loss describes money, rather than affordability, financial harm or gambling disorder. Clinical associations do not establish accuracy or a harm threshold. This bounded search provides methodological examples across survey, operator and treatment settings; it does not validate every financial family variant or accounting convention.
synthesis.things_to_consider_1: Specify formula, sign convention, currency, price basis, observation window and whether the output concerns a person, account, activity, household or population.
synthesis.things_to_consider_2: Report product/account coverage and handling of bonuses, free bets, cash-outs, refunds, transfers, unsettled bets and balances; unspecified rules are evidence gaps.
synthesis.things_to_consider_3: Distinguish stakes minus winnings from turnover, deposits minus withdrawals and income-normalised ratios; annual-average and directly observed monthly loss differ.
synthesis.things_to_consider_4: Describe recall aids, missingness, zeros/winnings and outlier handling; correlation with records does not guarantee agreement.
synthesis.things_to_consider_5: Interpret loss alongside resources and consequences when relevant; monetary loss alone does not measure harm, affordability or diagnosis.
